                                             PROJECT NO. 58482

 LARGE LOAD DEMAND                                           §      PUBLIC UTILITY COMMISSION
 MANAGEMENT SERVICE                                          §               OF TEXAS


    NRG ENERGY, INC.’S COMMENTS IN RESPONSE TO STAFF’S QUESTIONS

       NRG Energy, Inc. (NRG) appreciates the opportunity to provide comments in this project

on the Public Utility Commission of Texas (PUCT) Staff’s questions for comment1 regarding large

load demand management services to implement Public Utility Regulatory Act (PURA)2

§ 39.170(b) adopted by the Texas Legislature through Senate Bill 6 (SB6) in the 89th Legislative

Session.3 NRG is the parent company of established retail electric providers (REPs) and power

generation companies (PGCs) in the competitive electricity markets in Texas.

                                            I.       INTRODUCTION
       The development of large loads in Texas presents both significant challenges and

opportunities for the state. The demand management service for large loads that PURA § 39.170(b)

requires the Commission to develop is one of the key tools that can both manage those challenges

and create opportunities for large loads. NRG supports development of an “as-needed” service to

address “anticipated emergency conditions” based on anticipated Energy Emergency Alerts

(EEAs) and transmission emergencies, which will necessarily also meet the statutory directive for

the service to assist with maintaining reliability during extreme weather events. The Commission

should set a maximum duration limit for the service (i.e., 72 hours) and should request information

from data centers and other large loads to help determine a reasonable budget for the program.

Quantities could be determined using a similar methodology as (and as part of) the annual process



       1
           Project No. 58482, Staff Questions for Comment (March 23, 2026).
       2
           Tex. Util. Code §§ 11.001-66.016 (PURA).
       3
           89th Tex. Leg., R.S., Senate Bill 6 (SB6), § 2 (effective Jun. 20, 2025) (codified in PURA § 37.0561).
 PROJECT NO. 58482 – LARGE LOAD DEMAND MANAGEMENT SERVICE


that ERCOT uses for ancillary services. Technical details related to testing, qualification, and

performance could be worked out in the ERCOT stakeholder process.

       In addition, NRG supports the Commission including direction in this rulemaking on the

implementation of PURA § 39.170(a), to ensure that ERCOT and interconnecting utilities have

guidance on how to implement that provision in a way that does not interfere with the development

of new co-located generation resources in private use networks from continuing to provide service

to its co-located load during a grid emergency.

       NRG responds to Staff’s specific questions below.

                          II.     RESPONSES TO STAFF QUESTIONS

QUESTION 1:        Of the two options described in the attached slides, an as-needed service or
                   a seasonal service, which is the better option to implement PURA §
                   39.170(b) and why?

       NRG Response: NRG recommends development of the “as-needed” option for the

reliability service PURA § 39.170(b) directs the Commission to establish, given the potential for

extremely high costs for the seasonal option, which presumably would require a capacity payment

every hour of the applicable season. Large loads eligible for this service operate high value

processes that require near continuous consumption of electricity. To encourage them to reduce

demand when called on by ERCOT at any time during the applicable season, the compensation

would need to reflect the risk of lost revenue and the high cost of backup generation, which

suggests that the compensation would need to be very high to reserve large load curtailment

capability for an entire season. In other words, to reserve this demand reduction capability for all

hours of a season, the large load will likely require significant compensation to assume this risk of

deployment.

       A more targeted approach, as described in the “as-needed” option, should result in much

lower costs since each participating large load can narrow their opportunity cost and risk of


NRG COMMENTS RE: STAFF QUESTIONS                                                             2
 PROJECT NO. 58482 – LARGE LOAD DEMAND MANAGEMENT SERVICE


curtailment to the narrower time period covered by each of ERCOT’s procurements. As part of a

design of an “as-needed” option, NRG recommends the Commission set a maximum deployment

duration of 72 hours to provide certainty to large loads participating in this service. This certainty

is important for the large load customer so that the customer can assess the technology and

characteristics of their backup generation facilities compared to the performance requirements of

the product.

        In addition, the Commission should direct ERCOT to adopt clear rules for qualification,

procurement, dispatch, and settlement of the “as-needed” service, well in advance of the

implementation and procurement of this service, to maximize participation. In prior procurements

for Contracts for Capacity for demand response capacity, ERCOT released the details of the

qualification without sufficient time prior to procurement to allow for participants to adequately

respond.4 The Commission and ERCOT can avoid this outcome by solidifying the rules for the

program well in advance.

        Lastly, the Commission should consider setting limits on both (i) the number of

procurements ERCOT can make during a program year (potentially set each year following

ERCOT’s annual analysis of the anticipated need for the service) and (ii) how close together these

procurements can be, considering both the proposed procurement lead time (i.e., at least 3 business

days) and any event duration limitations the Commission adopts (which NRG recommends be set

to 72 hours). NRG believes that setting these limitations could be helpful to balance program

budget considerations with participating customers’ business operations continuity and certainty.




        4
          M-A050324-01 Notice Regarding Forthcoming Issuance of Request for Proposals for Capacity for Summer
2024 under ERCOT Protocols § 6.5.1.1(4) (releasing the request for proposal on May 8, 2024, with proposals due by
June 13, 2024).



NRG COMMENTS RE: STAFF QUESTIONS                                                                        3
 PROJECT NO. 58482 – LARGE LOAD DEMAND MANAGEMENT SERVICE


QUESTION 2:        PURA § 39.170(b) states the commission must require ERCOT to develop
                   a reliability service to be deployed in the event of an anticipated emergency
                   condition. PURA § 39.170(b)(1) states the rules governing the new service
                   must specify the periods when the service may be used to assist with
                   maintaining reliability during extreme weather events.

               a. Does PURA authorize ERCOT to deploy the new service in circumstances
                  other than extreme weather events? If yes, what kind of events?

       NRG Response: Yes. PURA § 39.170(b) requires the service to be deployed in the event of

an “anticipated emergency condition,” which may occur either during or outside of an extreme

weather event. While PURA § 39.170(b)(1) requires that the rule governing the service “specify

the periods when the service may be used to assist with maintaining reliability during extreme

weather events,” the statute does not limit the use of the service for extreme weather events, and

those events, to the extent they cause an anticipated emergency condition, would already be

covered by a service that is designed to address “anticipated emergency conditions.” In other

words, if the Commission focuses on developing a service to be deployed in the event of an

“anticipated emergency condition,” the service will necessarily aid in maintaining reliability

during extreme weather events, as required by the statute. But, there is nothing in the statute that

requires the Commission to limit the “anticipated emergency conditions” to only those related to

extreme weather.

       In developing the technical details of the program, the Commission and ERCOT will need

to work through the exact trigger for a procurement of an “as needed” service to ensure that the

service will be available and deployed for actual emergency conditions (i.e., during an EEA), since

both the procurement (at least 3 business days, as proposed by Staff) and notice (24 hours) must

occur in advance (i.e., for an “anticipated” emergency). For example, the procurement trigger

could be an operating condition notice or watch, but in any event, should be timed such that

ERCOT does not either over- or under-procure the service. An additional consideration for the



NRG COMMENTS RE: STAFF QUESTIONS                                                            4
 PROJECT NO. 58482 – LARGE LOAD DEMAND MANAGEMENT SERVICE


Commission in defining the procurement triggers is how this program may interact with other,

shorter notice programs, such as Emergency Response Service.


                   b. Should the commission define “extreme weather event” and, if so, how
                      should it be defined?

        NRG Response: No. NRG recommends the Commission focus on the deployment of the

service in anticipation of an emergency condition, which will cover all situations for the use of the

service, including any extreme weather events that threaten reliability (e.g., create a potential for

loss of load) and thus trigger the need for the service. NRG recommends against adopting a

requirement to deploy the service in all “extreme weather events” as defined under PURA5 and the

Commission rules6 for purposes of disconnection moratoriums and payment plans, as those

definitions are broad and can include many days where there is no realistic threat of a reliability

event (such as any time a heat advisory has been issued on a particular day or the previous two

days). Instead, the Commission should use expected EEAs or transmission emergencies as

anticipated emergency conditions and make deployment of the service contingent on ERCOT’s

expectation that those conditions will occur in the next 24 hours.




         5
           PURA § 39.101(h) (“For purposes of this subsection, ‘extreme weather emergency’ means a period when:
(1) the previous day's highest temperature did not exceed 32 degrees Fahrenheit and the temperature is predicted to
remain at or below that level for the next 24 hours according to the nearest National Weather Service reports; or (2)
the National Weather Service issues a heat advisory for any county in the relevant service territory, or when such an
advisory has been issued on any one of the previous two calendar days.”).
        6
            E.g., 16 Tex. Admin. Code (TAC) § 25.483(j)(1) (defining the term similarly to the statutory definition).



NRG COMMENTS RE: STAFF QUESTIONS                                                                              5
 PROJECT NO. 58482 – LARGE LOAD DEMAND MANAGEMENT SERVICE


QUESTION 3:        PURA § 39.170(b)(3) states the rules governing the new service must
                   prohibit participation by any large load customer that curtails in response
                   to the wholesale price of electricity, as determined by ERCOT, or that
                   otherwise participates in a different reliability or ancillary service. PURA
                   § 37.0561(e)—which allows ERCOT to direct a large load customer with
                   onsite backup generation to either curtail its load or deploy its backup
                   generation under certain circumstances—states that a large load customer
                   with onsite backup generation may participate in a service authorized by
                   PURA § 39.170(b).

               a. What type of qualification is necessary to show that it may take a large load
                  customer 24 hours to ramp down safely?

       NRG Response: The Commission should direct ERCOT to implement testing procedures

to qualify large loads for this program that demonstrate their ramp down capabilities and timing.

ERCOT has testing procedures in place today to qualify loads for other services,7 and those

procedures were developed in the ERCOT stakeholder process, rather than in Commission rule.

Notably, the only Commission rule addressing a demand response service is the Emergency

Response Service rule, and that rule sets broad guidelines and policies (such as budget and general

qualification requirements), while leaving the details to the ERCOT stakeholder process.8 NRG

suggests that a similar approach makes sense for the large load demand management service.


           b. What specific prohibitions not enumerated in PURA § 39.170(b), if any, should
              apply to participation in the new service?

       NRG Response: The Commission’s rule should require ERCOT to ensure that any onsite

backup generation facilities used by large load customers to provide this product can operate for

multiple days to remove the load from the ERCOT system (e.g., taking into account environmental

permit limitations and fuel supply). If the large load customer cannot demonstrate that its backup

generation facilities can run for the required maximum duration limit (which NRG recommends

be set at 72 hours), then that customer should not be able to participate, unless they demonstrate

that they can and will curtail the load for the maximum duration.



NRG COMMENTS RE: STAFF QUESTIONS                                                           6
 PROJECT NO. 58482 – LARGE LOAD DEMAND MANAGEMENT SERVICE


                 c. Should participation in price responsiveness to transmission scarcity such
                    as four coincident peak (4CP) or a successor methodology preclude
                    participation in the new service?

        NRG Response: Yes. Separately, in Project No. 58484, NRG is recommending the

Commission adopt a transmission cost allocation mechanism that eliminates the ability of large

loads to shift costs onto residential customers. As part of the effort to prevent cost shifting and

ensure that large loads appropriately contribute to transmission costs as required by SB6, the

Commission should not reward large loads that respond to 4CP (or a successor methodology) to

avoid transmission cost allocation with a payment for that response as part of the PURA §

39.170(b) demand management service.


                 d. Participation in price responsiveness to transmission scarcity such
                    as 4CP may often look like price-responsiveness to energy prices. Since
                    price-responsive loads will already be precluded from participation, the
                    rule may not need to require that ERCOT separately determine whether a
                    load was responding to energy prices or 4CP and instead can specify that
                    loads that respond to market signals (whether based on energy prices or
                    transmission scarcity signals) will be precluded from participation. As
                    suggested above, technical details regarding qualification should be
                    worked out in the stakeholder process at ERCOT. Should the commission
                    define “curtailment in response to wholesale price of electricity” and, if so,
                    how should it be defined?

        NRG Response: No. ERCOT already has effective processes to detect and measure whether

loads are price responsive.9 These same processes could be leveraged to determine which loads

should be excluded from eligibility for the PURA § 39.170(b) demand management program, on

the basis of having curtailed in response to the wholesale price of electricity or transmission

scarcity. With that said, one complexity that ERCOT will need to address is how to determine

initially (for the first few years of the program) whether a large load customer has been responsive


        9
          See, e.g., 2025 Annual Report on Demand Response in the ERCOT Region (Jan. 30, 2026) (describing how
ERCOT determines price responsiveness of loads from surveys to load serving entities, as well as from meter data),
available at: https://www.ercot.com/misdownload/servlets/mirDownload?doclookupId=1188179018.



NRG COMMENTS RE: STAFF QUESTIONS                                                                         7
 PROJECT NO. 58482 – LARGE LOAD DEMAND MANAGEMENT SERVICE


to price (or 4CP), as many of these large loads will be new customers without usage history. NRG

recommends that the specifics related to qualification (including how to determine price

responsiveness) would be better addressed in the ERCOT stakeholder process than in a

Commission rule.


QUESTION 4:        How should the target quantity, budget, and price be set for the new
                   service?

       NRG Response: Given the importance and impact of the cost of this service, NRG

recommends the Commission collect information from large loads, especially data center

customers, through an ERCOT request for information (RFI) on the prices large loads would need

to receive to encourage their participation. This will inform the Commission on an effective budget

and price cap. In developing the budget and price cap for the program year, the Commission also

may want to consider establishing a per-procurement budget, based on anticipated procurements

during the year. To establish procurement quantities, ERCOT could conduct an assessment on

optimal procurement quantities to resolve emergency conditions, with a reasonable probability of

occurrence using SERVM modeling, as part of the annual ancillary service determination.


QUESTION 5: What additional information should the Commission consider in its
              implementation of PURA § 39.170(b)?

       NRG Response: In order to minimize the cost impacts on retail electric providers (REPs)

and other load serving entities (LSEs), the Commission and ERCOT should consider an alternative

settlement mechanism for this service compared to what is used for typical settlement charges

today. If, as NRG has recommended, the Commission adopts an “as needed” option for this service,

the alternative mechanism should spread out charges over an extended period rather than assess

charges only during the time of deployment. Otherwise, significant costs would be charged to LSEs

and REPs over a matter of days and could ultimately be financially burdensome to customers, as


NRG COMMENTS RE: STAFF QUESTIONS                                                           8
 PROJECT NO. 58482 – LARGE LOAD DEMAND MANAGEMENT SERVICE


those LSEs would need the ability to recover the costs. One option would be to collect a fee from

LSEs over the course of the year to fund the program. Payments to large loads during procurement

could draw down from the fund and could be capped to not exceed the total amount in the fund. If

the service is not deployed with sufficient frequency to deplete the fund, excess funds collected

compared to a pre-determined fund maximum, equal to the annual program budget, could be

refunded to loads in a similar way as the Balancing Account for Congestion Revenue Rights.10


QUESTION 6:           PURA §39.170(a) states: The commission shall require the independent
                      organization certified under Section 39.151 for the ERCOT power region
                      to ensure that each electric cooperative, transmission and distribution
                      utility, and municipally owned utility serving a transmission-voltage
                      customer develops a protocol, including the installation of any necessary
                      equipment or technology before the customer is interconnected, to allow
                      the load to be curtailed during firm load shed. The electric cooperative,
                      transmission and distribution utility, or municipally owned utility shall
                      confer with the customer to the extent feasible to shed load in a coordinated
                      manner. This subsection applies only to a load interconnected after
                      December 31, 2025, that is not: (1) Load operated by a critical load
                      industrial customer, as defined by Section 17.002; or (2) Designated as a
                      critical natural gas facility under Section 38.074. Should the Commission
                      include in this rulemaking a directive implementing PURA §39.170(a)?

       NRG Response: Yes. The Commission should clarify that PURA §39.170(a) only imposes

load shed requirements on large load customers that are consuming electricity from the ERCOT

system. This section of SB6 was necessary to ensure large loads interconnected after December

31, 2025, participate in firm load shed to help alleviate emergency conditions resulting from

transmission security issues or inadequate supply to meet system demand—i.e., to ensure that new

large loads would not be prioritized over the average Texan during grid emergencies. However,

many data center customers have indicated a desire to co-locate with new generation in order to

maximize reliability for their site and contribute to the reliability of the ERCOT system by



       10
            See ERCOT Protocols, Section 7.6.



NRG COMMENTS RE: STAFF QUESTIONS                                                           9
 PROJECT NO. 58482 – LARGE LOAD DEMAND MANAGEMENT SERVICE


removing their load from the ERCOT grid during such emergencies, which helps to mitigate public

concerns with both affordability and reliability issues. During a grid emergency, these large loads

would not be a “load” at all, from the perspective of the ERCOT grid, because, consistent with

how private use networks have operated for years, they would be consuming power from on-site

generation rather than the ERCOT system.


       To incentivize and encourage these arrangements, and to implement the statute as written,

the Commission must ensure that the firm load shed requirements in PURA § 39.170(a) only apply

to large loads that are consuming from the ERCOT system and contributing to the emergency

conditions, as intended by SB6. If a large load customer is being served by new co-located

generation, which was likely funded by the large load customer for its own use to help mitigate

the impacts of these exact scenarios, and not consuming from the ERCOT system, the customer’s

load should not be subject to firm load shed. This is consistent with the treatment for all existing

co-generation and private use network arrangements that have been developed over the past 40

years, which exceeds 18,000MW.11


       Further, SB6 clearly differentiated between co-locating large loads with existing generation

(previously available to the ERCOT system) versus new generation being built to primarily serve

the co-located customer. SB6 imposes a specific process, in PURA § 39.169, to evaluate and

approve the former (but not the latter) arrangement, including by allowing the Commission to

impose as a condition of approval that the existing generation be made available to the grid in

anticipation of a grid emergency. But, importantly, that condition can be imposed only after

completing the process set out in PURA § 39.169 and only if the conditions are necessary to



       11
            https://www.ercot.com/misdownload/servlets/mirDownload?doclookupId=1207842497



NRG COMMENTS RE: STAFF QUESTIONS                                                            10
 PROJECT NO. 58482 – LARGE LOAD DEMAND MANAGEMENT SERVICE


maintain system reliability. If the Commission were to interpret PURA § 39.170(a) to allow utilities

to disconnect a large load customer in a private use network with new generation and to require

that the new generation be dispatched to the ERCOT grid during firm load shed, then the

Commission would effectively be subjecting co-locations with new generation to the same

condition that can be applied to co-locations with existing generation as part of the PURA § 39.169

process, but without any process or evaluation. This would frustrate the clear intent of the

Legislature in distinguishing these two scenarios.12 Thus, treating these two types of co-located

arrangements the same during firm load shed is not appropriate.


       During firm load shed conditions, the reliability impact to the ERCOT grid is solely related

to the load that is being consumed from the ERCOT system. Co-located generation is registered

as part of a private use network, which the ERCOT Protocols define as “an electric network

connected to the ERCOT Transmission Grid that contains Load that is not directly metered by

ERCOT.”13 The ERCOT Protocols similarly define the term “Load” in terms of the “energy in

MWh delivered” at a “specified point” on the “system.”14 Thus, to be load at all, there must be a

delivery of energy from the ERCOT system to the site (i.e., it must be a net importer of electricity),

and the operational and financial treatment of large load with co-located generation is based on its

net impact to the ERCOT system. The implementation of rules for PURA § 39.170(a) should

preserve this treatment. Forcing a co-located large load to relinquish any new generation built for

020126_Nodal.docx

NRG COMMENTS RE: STAFF QUESTIONS                                                                           11
 PROJECT NO. 58482 – LARGE LOAD DEMAND MANAGEMENT SERVICE


its own purpose is not supported by SB6 and would create a strong disincentive for data centers to

develop grid-friendly sites.



                                      III.    CONCLUSION

       NRG appreciates the Staff’s consideration of its comments in response to the questions

regarding the large load demand management services, as well as the requirements in PURA §

39.170(a), adopted via SB6 from the 89th Legislative Session.

                    NRG ENERGY, INC.’S EXECUTIVE SUMMARY

  •   NRG supports development of an “as-needed” service to address “anticipated emergency
      conditions” based on anticipated Energy Emergency Alerts (EEAs) and transmission
      emergencies, which will necessarily also meet the statutory directive for the service to
      assist with maintaining reliability during extreme weather events.
          o Procurement details will need to be worked out to ensure that the service is
              deployed in time for an actual emergency (e.g., EEA), but procurement could be
              based on ERCOT’s issuance of an operating condition notice or watch.
  •   The Commission should set a maximum duration limit for the service (i.e., 72 hours) and
      should request information from data centers and other large loads to help determine a
      reasonable budget for the program. The Commission may also want to establish a per-
      procurement budget.
  •   The Commission should also consider imposing limitations on the number of procurements
      per program year (perhaps based on ERCOT’s annual assessment of how many
      procurements it anticipates needing), as well as on how close together in time those
      procurements can be (i.e., to avoid back-to-back deployments).
  •   Technical details regarding qualification of loads—including determining if those loads are
      “price responsive”—should be worked out in the ERCOT stakeholder process, similar to
      how the Commission rule treats Emergency Response Service (by setting the budget and
      broad policies, but leaving the details to ERCOT Protocols).
          o The Commission should clarify, though, that response to transmission scarcity (i.e.,
              4 coincident peak or whatever replacement methodology the Commission adopts
              in Project No. 58484) also will qualify as price responsiveness.
          o ERCOT has current methodologies for determining the price responsiveness of
              loads (including to 4CP) and should leverage those methodologies for this purpose
              as well, though there may be some complexity initially to deal with the new large
              loads that seek to participate in the program.
  •   In order to minimize the cost impacts on retail electric providers (REPs) and other load
      serving entities (LSEs), the Commission and ERCOT should consider an alternative
      settlement mechanism for this service compared to what is used for typical settlement
      charges today by ERCOT, in order to spread the charges out over a longer timeframe.
  •   The Commission should clarify that PURA §39.170(a) only imposes load shed
      requirements on large load customers that are consuming electricity from the ERCOT
      system. If a large load customer is being served by new co-located generation, which was
      likely funded by the large load customer for its own use, and not consuming from the
      ERCOT system, the customer’s load should not be subject to firm load shed.

OUESTION 2:        PURA § 39.170(b) states the commission must require ERCOT to develop
                   a reliability service to be deployed in the event of an anticipated emergency
                   condition. PURA § 39.170(b)(1) states the rules governing the new service
                   must specify the periods when the service may be used to assist with
                   maintaining reliability during extreme weather events.

               a. Does PURA authorize ERCOT to deploy the new service in circumstances
                  other than extreme weather events? If yes, what kind of events?

       NRGResponse: Yes. PURA § 39.170(b) requires the service to be deployed in the event of

an "anticipated emergency condition," which may occur either during or outside of an extreme

weather event. While PURA § 39.170(b)(1) requires that the rule governing the service "specify

the periods when the service may be used to assist with maintaining reliability during extreme

weather events," the statute does not limit the use of the service for extreme weather events, and

those events, to the extent they cause an anticipated emergency condition, would already be

covered by a service that is designed to address "anticipated emergency conditions." In other

words, if the Commission focuses on developing a service to be deployed in the event of an

"anticipated emergency condition," the service will necessarily aid in maintaining reliability

during extreme weather events, as required by the statute. But, there is nothing in the statute that

requires the Commission to limit the "anticipated emergency conditions" to only those related to

extreme weather.

       In developing the technical details of the program, the Commission and ERCOT will need

to work through the exact trigger for a procurement of an "as needed" service to ensure that the

service will be available and deployed for actual emergency conditions (i.e., during an EEA), since

both the procurement (at least 3 business days, as proposed by Staff) and notice (24 hours) must

occur in advance (i.e., for an "anticipated" emergency). For example, the procurement trigger

could be an operating condition notice or watch, but in any event, should be timed such that

ERCOT does not either over- or under-procure the service. An additional consideration for the



NRG COMMENTS RE: STAFF QUESTIONS                                                            4
 PROJECT NO. 58482 - LARGE LOAD DEMAND MANAGEMENT SERVICE


Commission in defining the procurement triggers is how this program may interact with other,

shorter notice programs, such as Emergency Response Service.


                  b. Should the commission define "extreme weather event" and, if so, how
                     should it be defined?

        NRG Response: No. NRG recommends the Commission focus on the deployment of the

service in anticipation of an emergency condition, which will cover all situations for the use of the

service, including any extreme weather events that threaten reliability (e.g., create a potential for

loss of load) and thus trigger the need for the service. NRG recommends against adopting a

requirement to deploy the service in all "extreme weather events" as defined under PURA5 and the

Commission rules6 for purposes of disconnection moratoriums and payment plans, as those

definitions are broad and can include many days where there is no realistic threat of a reliability

event (such as any time a heat advisory has been issued on a particular day or the previous two

days). Instead, the Commission should use expected EEAs or transmission emergencies as

anticipated emergency conditions and make deployment of the service contingent on ERCOT's

expectation that those conditions will occur in the next 24 hours.

QUESTION 3:        PURA § 39.170(b)(3) states the rules governing the new service must
                   prohibit participation by any large load customer that curtails in response
                   to the wholesale price of electricity, as determined by ERCOT, or that
                   otherwise participates in a different reliability or ancillary service. PURA
                   § 37.0561(e)-which allows ERCOT to direct a large load customer with
                   onsite backup generation to either curtail its load or deploy its backup
                   generation under certain circumstances-states that a large load customer
                   with onsite backup generation may participate in a service authorized by
                   PURA § 39.170(b).

               a. What type of qualification is necessary to show that it may take a large load
                  customer 24 hours to ramp down safely?

       NRG Response: The Commission should direct ERCOT to implement testing procedures

to qualify large loads for this program that demonstrate their ramp down capabilities and timing.

ERCOT has testing procedures in place today to qualify loads for other services,7 and those

procedures were developed in the ERCOT stakeholder process, rather than in Commission rule.

Notably, the only Commission rule addressing a demand response service is the Emergency

Response Service rule, and that rule sets broad guidelines and policies (such as budget and general

qualification requirements), while leaving the details to the ERCOT stakeholder process.8 NRG

suggests that a similar approach makes sense for the large load demand management service.


           b. What specific prohibitions not enumerated in PURA § 39.170(b), if any, should
               apply to participation in the new service?

       NRG Response: The Commission's rule should require ERCOT to ensure that any onsite

backup generation facilities used by large load customers to provide this product can operate for

multiple days to remove the load from the ERCOT system (e.g., taking into account environmental

permit limitations and fuel supply). If the large load customer cannot demonstrate that its backup

generation facilities can run for the required maximum duration limit (which NRG recommends

be set at 72 hours), then that customer should not be able to participate, unless they demonstrate

that they can and will curtail the load for the maximum duration.

OUESTION 4:        How should the target quantity, budget, and price be set for the new
                   service?
       NRG Response: Given the importance and impact of the cost of this service, NRG

QUESTION 5: What additional information should the Commission consider in its
              implementation of PURA § 39.170(b)?

       NRG Response: In order to minimize the cost impacts on retail electric providers (REPs)

and other load serving entities (LSEs), the Commission and ERCOT should consider an alternative

settlement mechanism for this service compared to what is used for typical settlement charges

today. If, as NRG has recommended, the Commission adopts an"as needed" option forthis service,

the alternative mechanism should spread out charges over an extended period rather than assess

charges only during the time of deployment. Otherwise, significant costs would be charged to LSEs

and REPs over a matter of days and could ultimately be financially burdensome to customers, as

OUESTION 6:        PURA §39.170(a) states: The commission shall require the independent
                   organization certified under Section 39.151 for the ERCOT power region
                   to ensure that each electric cooperative, transmission and distribution
                   utility, and municipally owned utility serving a transmission-voltage
                   customer develops a protocol, including the installation of any necessary
                   equipment or technology before the customer is interconnected, to allow
                   the load to be curtailed during firm load shed. The electric cooperative,
                   transmission and distribution utility, or municipally owned utility shall
                   confer with the customer to the extent feasible to shed load in a coordinated
                   manner. This subsection applies only to a load interconnected after
                   December 31, 2025, that is not: (1) Load operated by a critical load
                   industrial customer, as defined by Section 17.002; or (2) Designated as a
                   critical natural gas facility under Section 38.074. Should the Commission
                   include in this rulemaking a directive implementing PURA §39.170(a)?

       NRG Response: Yes. The Commission should clarify that PURA §39.170(a) only imposes

load shed requirements on large load customers that are consuming electricity from the ERCOT

system. This section of SB6 was necessary to ensure large loads interconnected after December

31, 2025, participate in firm load shed to help alleviate emergency conditions resulting from

transmission security issues or inadequate supply to meet system demand-i.e., to ensure that new

large loads would not be prioritized over the average Texan during grid emergencies. However,

many data center customers have indicated a desire to co-locate with new generation in order to
